title: Digital-market conduct increasingly sits between competition and consumer law, making agency and coordinated redress central
source_unit: OECD, Competition and consumer policy in digital markets, OECD Roundtables on Competition Policy Papers No. 332
geography: Comparative digital-market policy and enforcement systems across OECD and partner jurisdictions

observations.period: 2026; digital conduct at the competition-consumer boundary

conduct_set.value: personalised pricing, recommendation systems, data-driven targeting, and interface design can influence consumer behavior and market dynamics

overlap.value: digital conduct increasingly raises concerns under both competition and consumer-protection frameworks

shared_objective.value: consumer welfare and meaningful consumer agency connect the two policy domains

observations.method: OECD comparative policy analysis and roundtable synthesis on competition and consumer policy in digital markets.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a policy synthesis rather than a prevalence estimate or causal market study; effects vary by conduct, market structure, consumer vulnerability, and enforcement regime.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, users with different digital literacy and resources, small firms, platform businesses, competition authorities, and consumer-protection agencies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Personalisation and platform design can improve relevance, convenience, and access when transparent, contestable, and aligned with user interests.

denominator.unit: OECD definition of consumer agency in digital markets

agency_definition.value: the meaningful ability to understand alternatives, make informed choices, and act on preferences

switching.value: consumer agency includes the ability to switch providers when appropriate

empowerment_competition.value: consumer protection and empowerment can support competition and innovation by enabling informed online choice

observations.method: OECD conceptual and comparative analysis of consumer agency, information, choice, switching, and market dynamics.
observations.uncertainty: Formal ability to switch does not establish low switching costs, usable alternatives, informed comprehension, or effective remedy for an individual consumer.
observations.subgroup: Consumers facing lock-in, personalized interfaces, bundled services, information asymmetries, limited digital skills, or weak alternatives.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some consumers value convenience over active comparison and may rationally delegate choices to trusted platforms or recommendations.

observations.period: 2026; digital practices creating simultaneous competition and consumer concerns

denominator.unit: digital-market conduct categories discussed in OECD comparative analysis

practice_set.value: drip pricing, misleading online choice architecture, AI-generated deceptive claims, tying, and interoperability restrictions

consumer_risk.value: practices can weaken transparency, autonomy, privacy, trust, or the ability to compare and choose

competition_risk.value: the same conduct can affect entry, market power, switching, innovation, and competitive conditions

observations.method: OECD mapping of practices that sit at the intersection of competition and consumer law.
observations.uncertainty: Whether a practice is harmful depends on implementation, context, countervailing benefits, market power, consumer understanding, and available remedies.
observations.subgroup: Online shoppers, users exposed to AI-generated claims, consumers in bundled or tied ecosystems, smaller competitors, and regulators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some design and bundling practices can reduce search costs or support product quality; enforcement should distinguish deception and foreclosure from ordinary innovation.

denominator.unit: comparative competition and consumer-enforcement coordination framework

coordination_need.value: joint advocacy, coordinated enforcement, and closer institutional cooperation are increasingly necessary in digital markets

distinct_mandates.value: competition and consumer authorities may cooperate while retaining distinct mandates

tradeoff.value: stronger product-safety obligations can protect consumers while potentially raising compliance barriers for smaller firms

observations.method: OECD comparative review of institutional arrangements, policy coordination, and enforcement implications.
observations.uncertainty: Coordination can improve coverage but may create jurisdictional conflict, delay, duplication, or uneven enforcement; the paper does not evaluate one universal institutional model.
observations.subgroup: Consumers seeking redress, small businesses, platforms, competition authorities, consumer agencies, data-protection bodies, and product-safety regulators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Separate mandates can preserve expertise and accountability; coordination need not mean merger or identical legal tests.

related_sources.claim: OECD roundtable summary on consumer agency, joint enforcement, drip pricing, choice architecture, and AI-generated deceptive claims.
OECD Consumer Finance Risk Monitor 2026 provides complementary financial-consumer risk and protection context.

boundary: This record adds a digital-market consumer-agency and institutional-redress route linking personalization, interfaces, pricing, switching, competition, trust, and enforcement coordination. It is not a consumer complaint microdata analysis, individual purchase panel, platform experiment, or causal estimate of consumer harm.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD 2026 paper, executive summary, intersection chapter, and coordination chapter were reviewed; consumer agency, digital conduct, practice overlap, and institutional-coordination claims were cross-checked.
